title: Open source AI is booming. Hugging Face explains who profits.
content:
Open source models are becoming more mainstream as enterprises, governments and startups alike rely on the promise of lower costs, more control, and more flexibility. But as increasingly capable models become more freely available, how do companies capture value? And with Chinese open models gaining ground, can American players keep up?
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan caught up with Irene Solaiman, Chief Policy Officer and SVP of Strategy at Hugging Face, about what startups need to know before building on open models, from choosing the right tools and infrastructure to navigating the trade-offs shaping the future of open AI.
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify and all the casts. You also can follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

report.summary: Open-source AI models are going mainstream across enterprises and governments, and Hugging Face's policy chief explains where the money actually flows — and whether US players can keep pace.
report.background: For years, frontier AI capability was locked behind proprietary APIs from a handful of labs. That changed as open-weight releases — Meta's Llama family, Mistral, and increasingly Chinese models like Qwen and DeepSeek — approached usable quality while remaining downloadable and self-hostable. The appeal is concrete: lower inference costs, no vendor lock-in, control over sensitive data, and the freedom to fine-tune for niche domains. Enterprises, startups, and now governments (concerned about sovereignty and procurement risk) have responded by building on open foundations rather than closed APIs. But openness creates a puzzle: if the weights are free, where does revenue come from? Meanwhile, Chinese labs have been unusually aggressive in releasing capable open models, turning open weights into a geopolitical and commercial lever. Hugging Face, as the de facto hub for open models, sits at the center of both the technical and policy debate — which is why its strategy voice is worth listening to.
key_points: Open models have crossed from hobbyist curiosity into mainstream enterprise and government procurement. The driving forces are cost predictability, data control, and the ability to customize weights rather than renting a black box. That shift is structural, not a temporary discount cycle, and it changes the default architecture for a lot of new AI products.

The central question is value capture, not capability. When weights are free, money migrates to everything around them: hosting and inference infrastructure, fine-tuning pipelines, evaluation, security, compliance, and support contracts. Hugging Face's argument is essentially that the moat is operational and ecosystem-based, not the model file itself.

Chinese open models are gaining real ground, pressuring US labs on price and openness. For startups, that widens the menu of cheap, capable base models; for American players, it raises the question of whether closed, high-margin APIs can defend share against free, good-enough alternatives.

Solaiman's practical advice for builders centers on choosing tools and infrastructure before committing, and being explicit about trade-offs: license terms, hardware requirements, maintenance burden, and safety obligations all differ across open models. Picking a base model is a long-term architectural bet, not a one-off download.

Policy is now part of the product landscape. Open-weight releases sit awkwardly inside emerging AI regulation, and Hugging Face has argued that transparency and reproducibility should count in open models' favor rather than being treated as a loophole.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a durable two-tier market: closed frontier models selling peak capability, and open models absorbing the long tail of cost-sensitive, customized, and regulated deployments. That compresses pricing power for mid-tier proprietary APIs and pushes labs toward either genuine frontier advantage or ecosystem lock-in. For developers, the upside is leverage — real alternatives, self-hosting, and portability — but also new burdens: you now own evaluation, safety, and infrastructure decisions that an API once handled. For regular users, the practical effect is cheaper and more varied AI features, plus more software running models locally or on regional infrastructure, which matters for privacy-sensitive products. The unresolved risk is fragmentation and uneven safety practices across freely distributed weights.
report.tools: Start with the Hugging Face Hub and Transformers for discovery and prototyping, then vLLM or Text Generation Inference for production serving. Ollama and LM Studio make local experimentation trivial on a laptop. For customization, look at PEFT and LoRA adapters, plus Axolotl for fine-tuning workflows. The Open LLM Leaderboard and community eval suites help compare open models honestly before you commit. Also watch licensing metadata and model cards closely — they determine what you can actually ship.
